title: Race, Disability, and Overlapping Barriers
before: How race, disability and institutional arrangements can interact in services and work, and why separate supports can miss a combined barrier.

turns.text: Race, Disability, and Overlapping Barriers looks at how racial expectations, disability access, and institutional arrangements can interact in DSD services and in workplace opportunity. The course draws on intersectionality, and it is careful to explain that this is about how conditions combine in people’s lives, not a list or a ranking of identities.

The opening example makes that concrete, because an accessible English document and an inaccessible translated image are offered as separate options. A reader who needs both the translated language and screen-reader access cannot use either one. Each feature might pass its own review, which is why the course asks what a review of each feature alone would miss.

That example is a good way into the concept itself. Intersectionality asks how interacting forms of power and exclusion can disappear when we use a single-category explanation. The course notes that its origins include Kimberlé Crenshaw’s examination of Black women’s experiences within race and sex discrimination frameworks. It is more than listing identities or adding up disadvantage.

The course also says something important about where problems sit. A racial or disability identity does not explain a barrier by itself. The better question is which requirement, assumption, resource, or decision makes the activity harder to access. That keeps the person’s strengths, preferences, and agency in the account, instead of treating their identity as the thing to repair.

Then the course follows the route a person actually takes. Finding information, responding, being assessed, and receiving a result are connected steps, and a barrier early on can change who appears in later information. In one practice case, a service discussion offers access support, but invitations circulate only through a familiar English-language network. You will decide on the best starting response to that situation.

Organizational structure plays a part, too, since one area may arrange access support while another handles outreach or response forms. Each task can look successful while the combined route stays unusable. The course asks you to state where the supports meet, so the right people can examine them together. Another case follows a translated, accessible invitation that leads to an English-only registration form.

The workplace example extends the same thinking to development. An employee can use the training room, yet project leads choose mentees through a familiar informal network. Racial expectations and inaccessible networking arrangements may both be relevant. You will consider how to examine that concern, and the course connects it to recruitment, onboarding, assignments, and advancement without assuming every stage works the same way.

I found the section on data especially useful. A difference in outcomes between groups can justify careful inquiry without establishing its cause. So you ask who is included, what the denominator describes, and whether the information is comparable. Small or incomplete categories can conceal variation and uncertainty, which is easy to lose sight of when a number looks definitive.

The course also guards against turning complexity into a ranking. No identity inventory can calculate someone’s hardship or predict their choices, and a person can meet a barrier in one setting and have an advantage in another. You can identify a possible barrier without deciding anyone’s full motive. Clear questions make a concern easier to examine without weakening its importance.

Near the end, you rewrite a single-category explanation using the training or registration case. You write what a disability-only or race-only account might notice and miss, then describe an interacting condition, a better question, and one limit of the evidence. The course also asks whether a proposed change simply shifts the burden to another step or another group.

As you start, think of a process in your own work that involves more than one kind of support, perhaps a translated notice, an accessible meeting, or an application. Where do those supports meet, and who would notice if they did not connect? Keep that example in mind, because the course will help you trace the whole route.

guidance.title: Conditions that combine
guidance.text: Intersectionality helps you see what a single-category explanation can hide. When race and disability are reviewed separately, each review may look complete while the person who meets both conditions still cannot get through. The aim is not to count identities or decide who has it hardest. It is to ask how forms of power and exclusion interact in a particular route, and what that interaction makes harder.

guidance.title: Checking the whole route
guidance.text: Think about a change you might propose for the training or registration case, or for a process in your own work. Does it address the connection that actually caused difficulty, or only one feature? Could it move the burden to a different step or a different group? Consider what information is still missing, and how you would avoid treating silence as a sign of success.
